poems.title: Spirit Track
poems.content:
I had a dream.

It started somewhere dark. Docks, warehouses, a place that almost felt like a camp. I was a prisoner, waiting for the right moment to escape. There were many others too.

When the conditions finally opened up, I ran with someone else. They were in the exact same situation as me, just slightly ahead, leading mostly by moving first, not by commanding. We crawled through a metal hangar close to the water and hid low to the ground. A patrol passed by. They had guns.

Somehow we managed to take their weapons, but we never had to use them.

Then something strange happened. First, that other person changed. Their body shifted and they looked like one of the workers or mercenaries from the patrol. A moment later, I changed too. My body followed. Suddenly we could stand at attention and blend in. We looked like we belonged.

We escaped in a vehicle that felt military. Two seats in the front, a large open storage area in the back. Later we switched to a locomotive, and once we were far enough away, the entire world began to transform.

Everything became bright and childlike.

I was no longer in a body. I was a soul, a small light. The other one was too. We were hovering above a landscape that felt familiar, like places I have seen in real life. A calm river, trees, birds in the sky, ducks in the water. At one point I paused and looked to the left, and I saw two swans gliding quietly.

There were children nearby, like on a school trip, riding on the locomotive. For some reason, we were assigned to them. It felt like we had a function, like we were both meant to watch over them. We felt like souls, almost like angels.

The other soul stayed closer to the children. It felt steadier, more responsible, more grounded. I would even call it slightly more masculine in presence. Not harsh. Not strict. Just compassionate and focused on keeping things safe.

I drifted away.

At some point I realized I was dreaming. I can control lucid dreams fairly well, so I could have changed the entire scenario. But I chose not to. I wanted to experience the dream as it was, because it was beautiful.

I was already flying around the locomotive, but then I saw the river more clearly, and I paused for a moment. It was absolutely beautiful. So peaceful and serene. I wanted to go. I flew harder, faster, and I felt pure joy. I watched the water move and splash in a trail behind me. I watched the swans and the ducks. I watched the trees and the light shimmering in the spring leaves. I felt free. I was laughing. I was surrounded by absolute beauty.

And something else was strange. I felt softer. Almost feminine, like a gentle caretaker, not in a physical way, but in a spiritual way. I knew that my smile was soft and pure, and that if I were to see myself as a person, I would see a young, happy lady. 

The other soul did not follow me. It stayed near the children, doing what it was doing. Watching. Guarding. Being present.

The only clear sentence it shouted to me from afar was simple: "Hey! We should not interfere with nature. We should observe it and guard it."

I did not argue. I did not rebel loudly. I was already at the river, and when I heard their voice, I agreed and slowly went back to the locomotive while looking back and around one last time. Later I even told that other guardian that I was chasing a child who wandered off, but I knew the truth. Nothing was wrong. I simply wanted to see the beauty up close.

I do not know exactly what it means. Maybe it was just my mind processing things. Maybe it was a part of me. Maybe it was something beyond me. Maybe it was God, trying to calm me by giving me an experience of beauty and freedom? But then, why the other person and soul? Why did I still have responsibilities? It didn't strip me of them, but they were different, given new form. And why did I see me as something more feminine, with a masculine counterpart who I don't know was me, a guardian angel or God Himself.

Unless I experience it again, I will never know. But when I was looking back at that view, I knew that I might not see this exact place again, but I was happy.

I was just a soul above a river, grateful that it was beautiful.

poems.title: The Small Book Under the Roof
poems.contentHtml:
I had a dream about my aunt again.

Not my aunt as she was exactly, and not her apartment as it existed in the world, but the way things appear in dreams when they are trying to tell the truth without being accurate representations of reality.

She died years ago, old enough for her death to feel less like an interruption and more like the natural closing of a long sentence. She was my grandmother's sister, but everyone would call her their "aunt", my father, myself, many people in my family, and even her friends. She was the quiet presence. She never married, she never had children of her own, but she would support everyone as if they were her own. She was always ready to give her all to support people who were dear to her.

And in my dreams, she keeps returning as something quiet and protective.

This time, the dream began in violence.

I do not remember what I had done, or what the world believed I had done, only that a part of it had turned against me. I was in some kind of house, or facility, or place where people are gathered before something terrible happens. There were already other people who were tortured there, killed. I was at the scene of a massacre. But a quiet voice told me to fall to the floor and pretend to be dead.

So I did.

There were others beside me, also lying still, also trying not to breathe too visibly. Then men came in with guns. They were looking for me, or for people like me. I remember the feeling more than the logic of it: the terror of being searched for, not as a person, but as a target. The need to make myself so still that even my body, even the smallest breath, would not betray me.

They looked. They checked. They moved on to search elsewhere.

Then came the people who carried the bodies away, to clean up the scene. 

At some point they lifted me too, or tried to take me somewhere bodies are taken when no one expects them to rise again. There was a sense that I would be burned, disposed of, erased as something already finished.

And something in me refused.

I moved before they could seal me away, and I escaped.

The dream changed then, the way dreams do. Suddenly I was running through my hometown. It was my hometown, but not exactly. The streets were familiar and wrong at the same time, as if memory had rebuilt them from older materials. It was destroyed, burning, as if a hurricane had passed through it and left behind a fire that wanted to consume everything it touched.

I knew where I had to go before I knew why.

My aunt's old apartment. It had been sold years ago, after she died, but that quiet presence told me to look for protection and safety there. 

In life, there had been no attic, no hidden place beneath the roof, no secret upper space where something important might have been kept. But in the dream there was. Her home had become larger than itself. Higher. Older. Almost sacred.

People were chasing me.

And there was one person, who had strange powers. He could break parts of the street with a movement of the hand, or send force through the air, or tear the ordinary world open with gestures that should have meant nothing. And he was only after me.

I remember this one exact scene when I suddenly saw a huge chunk of concrete being tossed just before my face. I looked to the right and I saw him. Standing menacingly before me. To this moment, I am still unable to describe him.

He was not death itself, but death would walk beside his shadow.
He was not evil itself, but evil gathered in every empty space he left behind.

And in the moment of it all, I gained powers as well, to aid me, to help me. I could only use them because somehow her presence was with me.

I reached the building she lived in. I do not remember climbing the stairs normally. If I did so, I would never have made it out alive. Instead, I remember breaking through, leaping upward, moving through walls or floors as if urgency had made architecture negotiable. That presence made it possible.

On the stairwell, just before her apartment, there was a small shrine for her. It was built and created by people who still remembered her. 

There were no grand altars, no statues. It looked just like one of those places people make when they cannot let someone vanish completely. Ones created just moments after someone's passing. A photograph, an image, flowers perhaps, candles, a small arrangement of memory. The kind of thing that says: someone lived here, and love did not know where else to go.

I stepped inside.

Her apartment was being renovated. Pearl-white paint was dripping from the walls, and tape still covered the old furniture to protect it from being swallowed by renovation. It looked as if the memory of her was slowly being erased, or at least hidden beneath something cleaner.

But high up, beneath the roof, there was a small old space that still carried the folk style she had loved so much. It was untouched, waiting to be found by someone who still remembered.

I reached there, and I found what I had come for.

A little book.

It was not exactly a diary. My aunt did not keep a diary like that, as far as I know. It was very small, almost like one of those pocket Bibles, but it was not exactly a Bible either, though it felt closer to that than to an ordinary notebook. It was small, worn, and deeply folk-like. A collection of private scriptures. Something between a prayer book and a record of things people used to know before everything became explainable.

I heard banging on the door. Whoever was chasing me was so close.
I opened it in the last possible moment.

There were notes inside, strange phrases, fragments that seemed half-Christian and half older than any language I speak. Not spells, exactly. Not magic in the childish sense. More like remembered speech. Words that had survived by being carried quietly from person to person, kitchen to kitchen, grave to grave. A chant, and a prayer in one.

Then I began to sing the exact text I was so desperately searching for, just moments before the door would finally break.

At first it was barely a melody. Something repetitive, simple, like a chant. Think of those Slavic folk songs, sung by women predominantly, overflowing with the wisdom of the people, supported by faith and rituals of the old.

And other people joined me, they came from everywhere around me. They were both spiritual and real. People who remembered me, and remembered my aunt.

And the one who had been chasing us felt it.

He could not come closer.

Strangely, there was no explosion of light, no final victory in the cinematic sense. No death, no dramatic defeat, no spears from the heavens or angels that would cast him away.

He simply stopped. The song made a boundary. Not a wall he could break, but a truth he could not enter.

After a while, he stepped back.

"Fine," he said, or something close to it. "I cannot proceed further. You won. I'll see you another time."

Then he closed the door and left.

I woke up with the strange feeling that dreams sometimes leave behind: not fear exactly, not comfort exactly, but the sense that something had been placed in my hands while I was not looking.

I keep thinking about that small book.

About the fact that it was hidden under the roof, in a version of her home that never existed, not really as it was. About the way I had to return to the place I came from in order to find it. About how the thing that saved me was not an argument, not a weapon, not proof that I had been misunderstood.

It was memory.

It was a voice.

It was the presence of someone quiet who, in life, would not have seemed like a figure of power at all.

There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from feeling misread by the world. Not merely disliked, not merely rejected, but made into something false. Treated as if the most frightened or wounded or defensive version of you is the whole truth. As if you are only the danger others see, and not also the longing, the tenderness, the discipline, the faith, the grief, the desire to be good.

Sometimes it feels like living with all of it requires a kind of death.

You learn not to move too much. Not to speak too fully. Not to let the wrong people see you breathing. You become still because stillness is safer than being interpreted badly. You stop fighting, trying to convince anyone that you are not the devil himself.

But some part of you waits.

Some part knows there is a room somewhere that remembers you differently.

Not as innocent in the childish sense. Not spotless. Not beyond shadow or anger or error. But whole. More than accusation. More than fear. More than the role you were given in someone else's story.

I wonder if that is why my aunt keeps appearing in my dreams. I still wonder if it is my mind that reaches for her, or if it is her communicating with me and being the quiet witness to the deepest parts of my soul.

It is as if some part of me believes that the dead who loved simply, who lived ordinary lives, who carried the small domestic holiness of kitchens and stairs and family visits, may still hold something for us. A thread. A blessing. A reminder that we belong to more than the moment trying to devour us.

I hope she is in heaven.

I still pray for her. Maybe that is all I can do. Maybe that is enough. Maybe prayer moves in both directions in ways I do not understand.

But I keep thinking of the song, that prayer, that chant she had written in that little book.

How it did not kill the darkness. It only made the darkness step back.

Maybe that is what protection is, more often than not. Not the end of all evil. Not a life where nothing ever returns to test you. Just enough remembered truth to make a boundary.



Just enough voice to say: not here.

Just enough inherited light to keep from being carried away as if you were already dead.



And somewhere, under the roof of a house that never existed, a small book remains open.

Waiting for the part of me that still knows how to reach for it.


A fragment of my aunt's old wall, memory arranged by hand.

poems.title: Shelter
poems.contentHtml:
After I posted my last text, I kept checking the comments.

Not obsessively. More like returning to a window after hearing something outside. There were kind comments, the ordinary small warmth of strangers recognizing something and naming it back.

But one comment was different.

It was only a name of a place. A square in a city.

My city.

No explanation. No sentence around it to soften the strangeness.

I clicked on the profile, searching for an answer. It was completely empty. It looked as though it had just been created. No photos, no history, no clues to tell me whether this was someone I knew or a complete stranger. Nothing to reveal their intentions. I read the name of the square again. I knew I shouldn't go. It defied all logic. But I couldn't stop thinking about that message. It sat in my mind like a hook.

So I went.

When I arrived, the square was full of people. They crossed through the space in all directions, carrying bags, checking phones, living their ordinary lives. But as I stood there, everything felt slightly out of sync, as if the world was separated from me by a pane of thick, invisible glass.

Near the center, by the monument, there was a man.

His hair was greasy in a way that made him seem unfinished. His clothes were dirty, smelling faintly of cold storage and old iron. A butcher’s apron. And the impression of a blade. Not openly displayed. But present.

I had SpaceHey open on my phone.

So did he.

"Hey," he said. His voice was ordinary, yet it seemed to bypass the air entirely.

"It was me," he said. "The comment."

He told me he wanted to show me something. I followed him.

We walked toward the outer parts of the city. As we walked, the geometry of the streets began to subtly fail. Buildings gave way to fields, the edges of the world blurring into a pale fog.

He spoke as we walked. He said he had read what I wrote. He liked the way I could hide something enormous inside something small and ordinary. "We are looking for people like you," he said.

I looked at him, trying to read his face. Who were they? And why did they need someone like me? He didn't explain. He just kept walking.

I was looking at his hand. The cleaver was clear now.

At some point I asked him to give it to me. I said I would feel safer if he was not the one carrying it. He hesitated, then, reluctantly, handed it over. The cold steel felt undeniably real against my palm. I could hurt him now, but I knew I did not want to. Holding the danger and refusing to become it. The blade grounded me as the fog grew thicker.

The place he brought me to was hidden deep among the trees.

It was a camp. Or a research facility. Or a film set. There were heavy canvas tents, pale lights, people moving with quiet, clinical purpose. My mind raced, trying to make sense of the words the butcher had spoken. We are looking for people like you. Were they looking for an actor? Someone who could play a specific role? But why a film set hidden in the woods? I couldn't understand what this place was for.

They led me into one of the tents.

They asked me to stand in the center. Behind my back, a large projector began to whir. It cast a blinding white light that swallowed my shadow. Something began to play behind me—a film, or a sequence of images. I could hear the faint flicker of the reel, I could feel the light shifting against my back, but I was not allowed to turn around to see it.

In front of me, a machine began to pull a strip of paper through its gears.

And just beyond the machine, in the dimness of the tent, sat a row of folding camping chairs. People were sitting in them. They didn't move. They just stared at me, their eyes reflecting the harsh light of the unseen film playing behind my back.

A line appeared on the paper.

Green.

Yellow.

Yellow.

Red.

I didn't understand it at first. Then, as the unseen images flickered behind me and the silent audience stared, the realization hit me. It was measuring my stress.

The moment I understood, a cold panic gripped my chest. The line turned completely, aggressively red. Entirely. I was being stimulated by whatever was playing behind me, and evaluated by the strangers in the chairs. My private terror, printed for the room.

The observers leaned forward slightly. The space closed in. The feeling of being watched became suffocating. I decided to become calm. Absurdly calm. I shoved the panic down, freezing my body into a statue.

The line turned green. The green of a lie told with a frozen body.

For a second, it worked. Then one of them noticed.

He looked at the paper, then at my chest.
"You’re controlling your breathing," he said.

As if the body, once accused, had decided to confess.

The reality of the room tilted. If I trembled, they had evidence. If I became still, I was hiding the problem. There was no color in which I was allowed to simply be a human being.

I ran.

I do not remember the exact mechanics of leaving. There are moments when the world, out of pity or exhaustion, stops insisting on continuity. The recollection of thoughts becomes blurry. One moment I was under the harsh projector. The next, I was somewhere else inside the larger complex, in a wooden shelter, stylized as a mountain lodge.

There were wooden walls, corridors, a fireplace, rooms where people sat and waited. It had the atmosphere of a place built to protect people from weather. It should have been comforting. I tried to hide there. I also tried to eat.

I sat down with a plastic-wrapped sandwich from a vending machine. I tried to perform the act of a normal person eating in a normal place.

But I was crying. Not beautifully. The tears came too quickly to hide. Some of them were from my old life, people who knew my name or my face or the outline of my existence, but not enough to enter it. They looked at me with that same distant concern. Okay, someone is crying. Why is he crying? I could almost hear their judgmental thoughts.

Someone went to get the specialists.
The ones from the machine.

I did not want no one to notice.
I did not want to sit alone with a sadness so visible that even strangers could read it from across the room.

But I did not want to be brought back under the light.
I did not want to be measured into safety.
I did not want my pain to become a room full of folding chairs.

Then, something outside began to break.

Wood splitting. Metal bending with a sick, high-pitched groan. The shelter shook violently, dust and splinters raining from the ceiling.

Outside, there was a monster.

It was almost human, but enlarged by rage or grief, a chaotic, thrashing mass of destruction. It tore through tables and structures around the shelter, destroying whatever was close enough to reach.

It could not enter. Or perhaps it would not.

The wall of the shelter was ripped open with a deafening crack. Wind and ash poured inside. The monster could not fit through the breach, but its massive, violent limbs thrashed blindly through the opening.

I scrambled backward in sheer terror. I wedged myself tightly between the remaining inner walls and the jagged shrapnel of the broken wooden beams. I hid in the wreckage, pressing my body against the floorboards, holding my breath as the chaotic mass outside roared and dismantled the world.

Through the violence of its own movements, the monster was caught in the wreckage it had made. A brutal, rusted machine, something like a heavy mower, cut into it. It was harmed by the consequences of its own blind, destructive swings.

Before it disappeared into the debris, it cried out. A pathetic, broken sound.

There was still a way to save it. That was the instruction.

I crawled out from between the broken walls into the quiet wreckage. I picked it up. After all the horror, the noise, and the size, what remained could fit in my hands. It felt fragile.

I carried it back inside the ruined shelter. In the back, resting in the gloom, was a machine different from the first one.

A terminal.

The first machine measured me.
The second might receive it.


...


I do not remember whether I reached the computer.

Maybe there was no need to remember.

There must be a difference between being measured and being understood. There must be a difference between being watched and being held.

I keep thinking about the man with the cleaver.

How frightening he looked. How easily I could have mistaken him for danger and nothing else. How he was the one who recognized my writing. How he led me to the place I did not want to enter. How he said they needed people like me, someone who could act, someone who could hide things. How he gave me the blade when I asked.

Maybe some guides do not arrive clean. Maybe some guides come from the part of life we would rather not touch. From kitchens, from blood, from slaughterhouses, from the old work of cutting one thing away from another. Maybe they do not save us by being harmless. Maybe they save us by handing us the danger and showing us we can hold it without becoming it.

I keep thinking about the monster too.

Grief, maybe. Anger.

The part of me that would rather tear the world apart than be placed beneath a light and explained.
The part that does not trust concern because concern has too often meant being reduced to what is wrong.
The part that learned to protect the wound by becoming larger and more frightening than the wound itself.

But I am also not sure if it was me at all. It makes me think it is something else.

But I know it was not only an enemy.

There are parts of us that become monstrous not because they are false, but because they have had nowhere else to live. And there are forms of help that make the monster worse, because they speak only to the symptom. The color. The behavior. The suspicious stillness. The evaluating stare while you cry over a terrible sandwich. The kind that watches you carefully and mistakes being watched for being held.

I do not know what happened to the part I carried.

I do not know whether I saved it.

But I remember the weight of it.

I remember the green line.

I remember the shelter.

I remember that the comment had only been a place name.

That comment is gone now.

But perhaps some messages are meant to look this way.

Some of them look like coordinates.
Some look like danger.
Some look like a man beneath a monument, waiting with a blade he will eventually place in your hands.

And somewhere inside, perhaps, there is still that terminal.

Waiting for the part of the monster that does not want to be monstrous anymore.

poems.title: The World That Doesn't Exist
poems.content:
There is a world I carry in my heart. I don't know exactly where it came from - perhaps from books read too young, from films whose light felt more real than the light outside the window, from some deep, stubborn sense of how things could be if people decided to take themselves seriously.

In this world, cities have souls. Streets are made for walking slowly. Coffee tastes like it was meant to be drunk in the company of someone who has time. People look at each other. Not through each other, not past each other - at each other, with the full weight of presence.

I have been looking for this world for a long time.

I have walked through old capitals and new ones, through squares that should have felt like something and didn't. I have sat in cafés in Valencia and on benches in Nicea and Malta, stood in the rain in London, got lost in the side streets of Prague, watched the light fall differently in Budapest than in Vienna than in Berlin than in Paris, felt the particular melancholy of Brussels, walked through Warsaw's reconstructed facades and thought about what it means to rebuild something from memory. Lisbon at dusk. Budapest at dawn. All the places that every guidebook promises will move you. 

The feeling didn't come. 

Or rather - it came, briefly, in fragments. A doorway. A statue. The smell of rain on old cobblestones. The subtle colors of French Riviera's sea. And then it dissolved again into the background noise of everywhere: the same glass storefronts, the same sounds, the same people moving through their days like they were completing a transaction they didn't remember agreeing to.

I began to understand that I was not looking for a place. I was looking for a frequency. Something that used to broadcast clearly and is now harder and harder to find - buried under the noise, under the speed, under the strange modern obligation to be everywhere and therefore nowhere.

What I was looking for, I think, was something like this.

A Sunday that moves slowly. A table with food made carefully, not efficiently. A conversation that goes somewhere unexpected and stays there for a while, unhurried, because neither person has anywhere more important to be. A love that is not a performance. A life that does not need an audience to feel real. People who know themselves well enough to be honest about what they want, and want something worth wanting.

I know how this sounds. I have heard the gentle diagnosis - you expect too much, the world is what it is, you have to meet people where they are. And maybe there is truth in that. But I also know this: at fifteen, I could already see the shape of the disappointment that was coming. Something in me understood, even then, that the world I was inheriting was not the world described in the books, not the world the architecture promised, not the world that the best of human thought had pointed toward for centuries.

I kept going anyway. I kept looking.

Because if I can want this - if this longing exists in me with such clarity and such persistence - then it cannot be only in me. I try to believe this longing cannot be mine alone. If I feel the frequency, I want to believe someone else must feel it too. It has to exist somewhere, in someone, waiting to be recognized.

This is the thought I return to. Not as comfort exactly - more as a refusal. A refusal to believe that what I am looking for is simply not there.

And yet.

I keep moving through a world that wears on me in ways that feel difficult to explain. I keep meeting people who speak of depth, but when closeness begins to cost them something, they reach more for confirmation than for truth. People who seem, from a distance, to be looking for the same things I am - depth, honesty, something real - and then, up close, turn out to be looking for a mirror. Someone to confirm them, not someone to grow with. I know the distance is not only out there. Some of it is mine too.

This is the loneliness that is hardest to name. Not the loneliness of being alone - that I can live with, I have made something of it. But the loneliness of almost. Of thinking: here, finally, someone who understands. And then watching them do something that makes it clear they don't, not really, not when it costs them something.

I don't say this with contempt. I say it with the particular exhaustion of someone who sees the pattern clearly, is tired of seeing it, keeps looking anyway, and keeps finding it in other people.

Too often, the world feels like an almost to me. I don't know how else to put it. Not evil — an almost. Tired of itself. And I cannot make my peace with it. And I am not sure I want to. Because making peace with it would mean giving up on the frequency I keep hearing, faintly, underneath all the noise.

So I come home.

My apartment is, genuinely, a good place - I want to say that without irony. There are books, games and gadgets I love. There is a desk where the light is so good in the mornings. There is a particular silence here that I have made my own. It is full, in its way. It is mine.

And yet I come back from the world - from the cities, conversations I observe but never quite enter, from parties I attend but I don't party at, from all the places that promised something and delivered something slightly less - and what I want, with a clarity that sometimes surprises me, is warmth and understanding. Not the warmth of a room. Something else. A presence already there when the door opens. Someone who would ask how my day was and actually want to know.

Instead, when I get home, I get under the covers. I pull the blankets around me and I let the quiet settle, and I give myself the warmth that the day didn't give me, that the world outside doesn't give me.

It is enough. Mostly it is enough.

But I will tell you the truth: I am more disappointed than I expected to be. I came in with a specific image of what life could look like, and the distance between that image and the everyday is something I feel every morning - and despite being an adult, have not yet learned to stop feeling.

I am still looking for the world I was promised. In small things. In the rare moment when something is exactly what it appears to be. In the stubborn, possibly foolish belief that if I can imagine it this clearly, it cannot be entirely imaginary.

I pull the blankets tighter.

And I keep looking - but more and more, I also try to build fragments of that world where I stand.

poems.title: The World That Doesn't Exist. Yet.
poems.content:
Something has shifted since I last wrote about the world that doesn't exist.

Not in the world outside, which remains, as ever, approximately what it was, but in the texture of my days. They are fuller now. Fuller and heavier, in the way that good things sometimes are.

I cook nearly everything at home now.

And I challenged myself to cook something that would seem incredibly simple and ordinary, but only at face value.

A lasagne. But not the kind that comes in a box, ready to heat and eat.

The kind that starts with scouting for ingredients in different stores and aisles. The one that requires research and planning. The kind that begins the night before, with a ragù that needs hours on the stove: low heat, occasional stirring, the smell of it slowly changing from sharp to something deeper, something that makes the apartment feel inhabited. The kind where the pasta is made by hand, rolled thin enough to almost see through. Where the béchamel has to be watched, whisked without stopping, because the moment you look away it catches on the bottom and the whole thing has to begin again. And one that leaves a mess to clean afterwards.

It took me most of a Saturday. I made mistakes. The first sheet of pasta tore. The ragù was too wet the first time I made it, and I had to learn why, too high a heat, too much liquid added too fast. I cleaned the kitchen twice. I stood at the stove longer than I expected, and my feet hurt, and I did not mind. And the worst part - I was unable to scroll through my phone while waiting, as my hands were covered in pasta.

When it came out of the oven, I let it rest for twenty minutes, the way the recipe said, even though I didn't want to wait. Then I cut into it and the layers held.

I ate it alone... But it was very good.

There is something I have been learning in moments like this, at the stove, or late in the evening with documentation websites open on one screen and something half-built on the other, debugging something that should work and doesn't, going back, trying differently.

The thing I am learning is this: effort is not the opposite of pleasure. Difficulty is not the opposite of meaning. The life I am building requires more of me than any life I have lived before. More patience, more precision, more tolerance for the gap between what I intend and what I produce.

And I am finding, slowly, that I do not want it any other way.

I carry my own body through its days. I cook for it, I wash its clothes, I put bandages on the small wounds that come from getting a little too carried away while cooking. I ask a great deal of it and it asks things back.

This is not a complaint. This is what it feels like to be alive on purpose.

But there are evenings.

After the kitchen is clean and the work is closed and the apartment has settled into its particular nighttime quiet — there are evenings when I make myself something to drink, something cold, something with fruit, something that requires just enough attention to feel like a small act of care — and I sit with a feeling I have learned not to rush past.

It is not unhappiness exactly. It is closer to... exposure. The awareness that all of this: the effort, the careful meals, the late nights spent on side-work... all of it is being done without any aid, any help, any support. And what if something goes wrong? Not catastrophically. Just ordinarily wrong, the way things go wrong: a bad week, a setback, an injury, a day when the uncertainty of everything presses too close and the apartment feels very quiet and very still.

Who will be there for me?

I do not ask this with despair. I ask it the way you check the weather before a long journey, not to be stopped by it, but because the question is real and deserves to be taken seriously. I am working towards something that requires a great deal of me, and I am working on it alone, and some evenings the aloneness has weight.

What I want, and what I have always wanted, what the world that doesn't exist was always really about, is not a lighter life. I do not want the effort to go away. I do not want the difficulty to be smoothed over, the demands softened, the distance between intention and result closed by someone else's presence. I want to carry my own weight. I have learned that I can.

What I want is someone carrying theirs, beside me.

Sometimes, words return to me from elsewhere. Someone recognizes something in them, names it back to me, and for a moment I can see that the warmth I was trying to describe is not mine alone.

But there is a quieter question that arises from this. Not: do they feel it? Feeling it is not rare. People feel it in the space between where they are and where they thought they would be. They feel it when something names what they could not name themselves. They feel it and describe it beautifully, precisely, with real intelligence and real pain.

The question I ask now is what they do with it.

Because there is a difference between longing for a life and moving toward one. Between being drawn to what someone represents and being willing to enter the actual difficulty of it. Between recognizing something as true and choosing it when choosing costs something. Perhaps some people recognize it as something they once had, or almost had, or chose to leave behind.

As for me, I cannot live in a way that would betray that world. I have learned to ask whether someone is already moving before I arrive. Whether their life has its own momentum. Whether they would still be building on a Saturday morning if I were not there to see it.

Someone who would not need me to be their better life. Someone who is already building one.

The lasagne lasted for longer than I thought. I ate it for lunch, reheated, and it was better each time — the layers settling into each other overnight, the flavors deepening with rest.

I have already started looking for the next recipe.

Perhaps something Asian this time. Something that will require most of a day, ingredients I will have to search for, techniques I will have to learn and fail at before I get right. Something that, when it works, will feel earned in a way that shortcuts cannot replicate.

I am still building fragments of the world where I stand.

And I am still cooking.

poems.title: A World Made of Bridges
poems.content:
I have written before about a world that does not exist. Or perhaps more precisely, a world that does not exist often enough around me.

A world of warmth, attention, slow rituals, honest presence, and small things done with care.

For a long time, I thought of it as something I was looking for. Something hidden somewhere beyond the noise. Something I might one day find whole, if only I kept walking long enough.

Later, I began to understand that if I could not find it whole, I would have to build fragments of it where I stood.

And strangely, that changed me.

Not all at once. Not dramatically. The world rarely changes a person in the way stories promise. It does not always arrive as thunder, or revelation, or a door opening at exactly the right moment.

Sometimes it changes through smaller things.

A meal cooked with more patience than necessary.
A room arranged with care.
A message answered honestly.
Or a plan made and kept.

A morning where you choose what deserves your attention, and a night where you realize that the choice mattered.

I began to see that building a world, even privately, does not remain private for very long. If it is alive, it reaches outward. It wants to be answered.

A world kept only inside the heart eventually becomes a museum. Beautiful, perhaps. Carefully preserved. Full of meaning. But still.

Untouched by anyone.

And I do not want the world in my heart to remain only beautiful.

I want it to become reachable.

I have always thought of myself as an introvert, and I still do. But I am beginning to understand that people themselves are not what exhaust me.

It is emptiness that does.

Rooms full of people with no bridge between us. Conversations that move without touching anything. Gatherings where everyone is present and yet nothing reaches anyone. In places like that, I can feel lonelier than I do on my own.

But when something real is allowed to pass between two people, the exhaustion changes.

Sometimes it disappears completely.
Sometimes it becomes warmth.
And sometimes it becomes a kind of energy I did not know I still had.

When I speak from something I genuinely love, it does not feel like performance. It does not feel like forcing myself outward. It feels more like opening a door and letting someone see the room inside.

A film. A game. A recipe. A piece of music. A strange project. An unrealistic idea. A thought I have been carrying for too long.

These things become easier to share when they are not used to impress anyone.

They become bridges.

And a bridge works both ways.

I give someone a fragment of my world, and they answer from theirs. For a moment, neither of us has to stand entirely alone inside ourselves. Something crosses the distance. Something small, maybe. Something ordinary.

But ordinary things are not small when they reach another person.

Someone left a comment that stayed with me — something about a man who could change the world, if only the masses would listen.

It touched the right place, but not quite the right frequency.

I do not think I want a podium.

There is something strangely shallow, at least for me, in the idea of speaking to a crowd only to be seen speaking. To turn personality into a broadcast, passion into a product to sell, depth into something tailored for applause.

I understand the temptation. Everyone wants to be heard. Some want to become the savior, the grand figure, the man who changed the world.

But I am beginning to think the world is not changed first by being spoken to from above. Maybe it is changed when one person becomes a little more trustworthy.

A little more present.
A little more willing to answer.
A little more careful with what another heart gives them.

And a little more aware of what they leave in return.

Maybe it is changed when someone learns that presence is not only something we ask for, but something we are responsible for.

This does not mean I have stopped wanting the deepest things.
I have not.

There is still a part of me that longs for love that does not have to remain symbolic.
For someone beside me not as an idea, not as a distant possibility, but as a fact, a choice.

I still want the house.
The shared table.
The morning.

The life where love has a body, a voice, and somewhere to rest its hands.

But I am starting to see that if I wait for only that bridge, I may forget how to build any others. And I do not want my heart to become a locked room, preserved perfectly for someone who has not arrived.

As there is a loneliness that disguises itself as loyalty.

It says: keep everything reserved.
It says: wait.
It says: do not give too much of yourself to the world, because the right person has not come yet.

And there is truth in being careful. There is wisdom in not giving sacred things to every passing hand.

But a heart that never opens does not remain pure.
It becomes unused, dormant.

And I do not want that either.

As tempting as it can be, a person can block the outside world completely, afraid to be hurt again, believing they can isolate themselves and build a world of their own.

I tried to become that person...

But something in me refused.
My own drive forced the windows open and let in the demanding wind of responsibility. It filled the sails before I was ready, pushed me toward the open sea, and seemed to say:

You wanted to build your world.
Then let the world be your canvas.

And perhaps that is what the next part of building means.

Not only making my own life warmer, more intentional, more accountable, more beautiful, more capable of holding what I value.

But making it reachable.

A message sent.
A plan made.
A movie night prepared.
A conversation entered honestly.
A small risk taken.
And a big risk taken.

An apology given before pride has time to decorate itself.
A little more trust placed in the world than the day before.

These are not substitutes for love.
But they are ways of remaining capable of it.

Because maybe love does not begin only when the right person arrives.
Maybe it begins earlier.

In the way we prepare ourselves to receive them.
In the way we learn not to turn every wound into a wall.
In the way we choose, again and again, to make the world less lonely where we stand.

Even if it hurts sometimes.

I used to think the world I wanted had to be built like a house.
A place of warmth, shelter, ritual, and rest.

And I still believe that.

But now I think it also has to be built like a bridge.

Something that reaches.
Something that risks the distance.
Something that says: there is a world here, if you want to cross.

And maybe not everyone will.

Maybe some will pass by.
Maybe some will stand at the other side and never take a step.
Maybe some bridges will lead nowhere.

But some will hold.
Some will be crossed.
Some will become the beginning of a road neither person could have built alone.
And perhaps that is enough reason to keep building.

Not because the world is already what I want it to be.

But because, sometimes, for a moment, two people can stand on the same bridge.
And what was once only carried inside one heart becomes real between them.

And the world inside your heart says:

You were never only waiting.

You were arranging the room.
You were answering the message no matter how tired you were.
You were learning how not to turn every wound into a wall.
You were placing one ordinary brick after another, even when no one was there to call it beautiful.

And perhaps that is how it begins.

Not with thunder.
Not with certainty.
Not with the whole world arriving at once.

But with one bridge that holds.

One person who crosses.
One moment where what lived alone inside you becomes real between two people.

And then the world is not imaginary anymore.
It starts to exist.

It is small.
It is fragile.

But it is here.

So make it your own.

title: A Better Life
content:
It may be true that I am starting from a worse place.

I am more alone than some people are. I have less support around me. I do not have someone’s steady presence at the end of the day, or a shoulder to lean on when the weight of memory returns. I have only myself to control myself and my triggers. Some people begin again with company. I begin again with myself.

But I am beginning again.

And that matters more than people care to think.


There are experiences that do not simply pass through the mind. They enter the body. They settle in the nervous system. They turn ambiguity into danger, distance into panic, silence into a threat. I know now that what brings out the worst in me is not love itself, not closeness itself, but uncertainty. Not knowing where I stand. Feeling that something essential is left unspoken. Feeling that someone is divided, half-present, half-committed, half-looking back at another life while asking me to stand still and endure it.

That is where my body remembers too much.

That is where tension enters. Freeze takes over my body. The need for clarity becomes stronger than it should be. And if I stay inside that kind of reality for too long, I do not become wiser or nobler for my patience. I become split. Exhausted. Reactive. Less like the man I know I can be.

I know now that empathy without boundaries can become self-betrayal. I know now that it is possible to care deeply and still be wrong to stay. I know now that some situations do not become healthy just because you pour more understanding into them. Some situations remain unhealthy because confusion was woven into them from the beginning.

And I stayed in some of them for too long.

I tried too long to be patient with things that were never mine to carry. I tried too long to make room for someone else’s unresolved past, someone else’s emotional chaos, someone else’s fear, someone else’s indecision, someone else’s life that was still tied elsewhere. I tried too long to call that compassion when in truth it was eroding my peace.

And it is true that I didn't help them. I know I made mistakes. I know I could have chosen earlier. I know I could have left earlier. I know I should have trusted the absence of peace sooner. I know I should not have allowed certain stories to drag on until they brought to life the most wounded and unstable version of me. And I tried numerous times, but for some reason, I still failed most of my tries.

But I will only take responsibility for what was actually mine.

    Not for someone else’s past.
    Not for someone else’s poor choices.
    Not for someone else’s chaos.
    Not for someone else’s inability to choose clearly.
    Not for someone else’s divided life.
    Not for someone else’s family comparing me to another man.
    Not for someone else’s confusion about what kind of future they wanted.

I will take responsibility for my mistakes. I will learn from them. I will grow wiser because of them. But I will no longer carry the entire moral burden of stories that involved more than one person, even if others will deny how much they hurt me as well.

There comes a point where maturity is no longer more understanding. It is saying, simply and without drama: yes, this hurt me, this was not healthy for me, and I do not want to live like this ever again.

That point has come for me.


I want to live a different life.

I want work and passions that give me room to build, to create, to move through life with dignity, and I am on my way. People reach out to me to collaborate, to reach new heights. I want to live in a way that is not shaped by chaos, not dependent on intensity, not tied to pain in order to feel meaningful.

I want to build a home with someone I love, and someone who chooses me clearly, and someone I can choose clearly.

I want to meet a person and know that there is only me and them in the picture. No emotional triangles. No divided loyalties. No compromises because of age, distance nor circumstances. No one living one life while promising another. No one secretly measuring me against somebody else. No one asking for patience while still standing with one foot in the past.

I want a relationship with milestones, with readiness, not endless confusion.

I want a life where clarity is not treated as pressure, where honesty is not treated as excess, where commitment is not treated as naivety. I want day-to-day life with someone whose world can genuinely start aligning with mine, right here and there. I want peace. I want consistency. I want warmth without chaos. I want love that does not slowly split me apart.

And I know now that I am allowed to want that.

More than that, I know I am capable of building it.

Because despite everything, I know who I can be.

    I know I can be calm.
    I know I can be loyal.
    I know I can be thoughtful.
    I know I can be gentle.
    I know I can be deeply committed.
    I know I can be a good partner, a steady presence, a good man to build a future with.

I have seen enough proof of that in my life.

People remember me warmly. People trust me. People reach out to me to talk, to create, to think, to build, to cooperate and work. People trust my guidance, because they know I mean good for them. I know I am not only the man shaped by his worst moments. I know there is more in me than that. There always was.

That is why I still believe in my future.

Not because I want revenge.
Not because I need the people who hurt me to finally approve of something.
Not because I want to spend my life proving someone wrong.

But because I want to live well.
Because I want to heal.

Because I want to build a life better than the chaos that nearly became my normal.

Maybe some people won the short game. Maybe they walked away with more support, more voices, more reassurance, more company. I walked away with shame, pain, loneliness, voices that ridicule me for even bringing certain situations to life. Or that I even care. But I care about people, and perhaps this is why bringing them pain hurts me as well.

But the long game of life is not decided by who tells the cleanest story first. It is decided by who builds something real.

And I will.

    I will build a life where I no longer beg ambiguity to become peace.
    I will build a life where I no longer wait to be chosen by people who are not truly free to choose.
    I will build a life where my values, my faith, my boundaries, and my need for clarity are not treated as burdens.
    I will build a life where love does not require me to abandon myself.
    I will build a life where no one has to walk on eggshells, and no one has to disappear in order to stay loved.

I am freer now than I was inside everything that slowly destroyed me.

Now I am on the outside.

And with time, self-respect, discipline, and the right choices, I will become even freer.

This story will not define who I am at my core.

It will define what I no longer accept.

And from that alone, a better life begins.

poems.title: Swan
poems.contentHtml:
There was once a swan who believed himself to be entirely white.

His feathers caught the light in soft layers, reflecting sky and cloud so gently that from a distance he seemed almost made of the lake itself. Those who paused by the lake's shore spoke softly of the grace of swans — of their purity, of the calm dignity with which they moved through the world.

In time, the swan had learned to believe such things about himself.

Each morning he lowered his head and drew his beak slowly through the white layers of his wings, smoothing them back into place. A swan must be white. That was simply how things were. The lake expected it, the sky reflected it, and every passing gaze seemed to confirm it.

For a long time, the swan believed this was exactly what he was.

He was gentle in the way some creatures are gentle when they are afraid of being seen too clearly. Where the water grew restless, he moved through it slowly, and the ripples softened around him. Other birds trusted such stillness. The swan knew how to make calm look natural. He knew how to drift close enough to be comforting, and far enough to remain unreadable.

He seemed at times to avoid the darker reaches of the lake, as though he sensed something unsettled there. He would turn slightly away, keeping to clearer water, and his movement alone was often enough to make others follow. Yet later he would return to those same places without explanation, as if the boundary had shifted — or had never truly been where it seemed. On rare occasions, something else surfaced: a small fracture in the stillness, a fleeting suggestion that the whiteness did not come as easily as it seemed. It passed quickly, like a ripple that closes before it reaches the shore.

For a while, no one thought much of this. The lake was large. Water changed. Light changed. And from a distance, the swan remained what he had always appeared to be: white, composed, easy to trust.

Until one day, while tending the feathers beneath his wing, something darker appeared between the layers.

At first it looked like a shadow cast by the water. He shifted, expecting it to disappear. But the shape remained, narrow and quiet beneath the white. The swan bent his neck further and saw that it was not a shadow at all.

It was a feather. And it was black.

The discovery did not arrive as a shock so much as unease, the way cold water slips slowly between feathers when the wind changes direction. The swan caught the feather gently in his beak and pulled. It came free with a small, sharp pain he had not expected.

He let it fall into the water and watched it drift away. The lake closed over the moment as though nothing had happened.

For a while, he felt relief. The white layers of his wings settled back into place, smooth and familiar. The lake reflected him just as it always had: a quiet white shape moving through still water.

But days later, while cleaning himself again, he found another dark line hidden deeper beneath the surface of his wing.

Then another.

Each time he found one, he removed it quickly. Sometimes he told himself it was only a stray feather, something that had never truly belonged to him. Sometimes he blamed the light, or the distortion of the water below. The lake was full of such small uncertainties. One could not trust every shadow.

And yet... the black feathers kept returning.

Some came easily. Others resisted, and when they finally loosened, they left a dull ache beneath the swan's skin. The discarded feathers floated quietly beside him before the slow current carried them away.

From the shore, nothing seemed to change.

The swan still moved with the same quiet grace. His feathers still shone pale against the darker surface of the lake. His whiteness did more than conceal him — it arranged the gaze of others before they had come near enough to question it. As long as no one looked too closely, everything seemed perfectly fine.

There were also times when something of the swan moved beneath the surface of things rather than across them. Not visibly — his white shape remained where it had always been, calm and composed at the center of the lake — but something else moved outward from him, quietly, through the water. A disturbance that could not be traced back to any single wing-beat. Signals that reached other birds from no direction in particular. Presences that watched without being seen. The water carried these things gently, the way it carries everything: without explanation, without signature.

The swan drifted on, unhurried and serene.

So he kept away from the shallows, where the water grew clear enough to reveal too much. He avoided the hour when the sun stood low and every detail sharpened. When other birds drifted nearer, he could be unexpectedly warm, drawing close enough for his whiteness to feel like shelter. He had a way of making nearness seem chosen, as if the quiet between them had always belonged there.

Yet if they remained too long, or looked too carefully, something in him would shift.

It was never sudden. The water would change first, almost imperceptibly — a small tightening of space, a pause where there had been ease. Then the swan would turn away, not abruptly, but just enough to unsettle what had begun to form. What had seemed like calm would thin, and what remained would no longer hold in the same way.

He wanted the calm he carried to be real. He wanted the stillness to hold. But beneath the white feathers, the darker ones kept growing. And the more carefully he removed them, the less clearly he could tell what belonged to him and what did not.

And so he continued, as he always had.

From time to time another dark feather appeared beneath the white layers of his wings. Each time, he concealed it beneath the pale ones, or removed it carefully and let the water carry it away. The work was quiet, almost invisible, leaving behind no trace that could be easily seen.

Sometimes, when the lake was perfectly still, the black feathers gathered around him for a moment before drifting apart again. The water moved them in small, patient circles, turning them slowly in the light. From above, they almost resembled shapes.

Petals.

Small dark flowers opening on the surface of the lake.

The swan never noticed them.

He drifted calmly across the water, white and serene as always, not knowing that the water around him had already begun to flower.

poems.title: Blackbird
poems.contentHtml:
There was a blackbird who could not forget the nest.

Not one particular nest that had once almost closed itself among the leaves, but its very shape — the inward form of shelter that comes before any place, any branch, any season. He carried it within himself before the first dawn, before the first attempt at song.

The blackbird did not build high. He felt no pull toward the empty sky. He chose lower places instead, closer to the ground, where light is not yet triumph but grace, where leaves know not only how to let brightness through, but also how to hold back the cold of too many gazes and the excess of wind. He knew that a nest is not its form alone. A nest holds warmth. And warmth is fleeting, so the nest must be lined well, without gaps, without cracks.

The blackbird built with seriousness, not with carelessness.

There were mornings when everything seemed simpler. The air carried the taste of moisture and a new beginning. The grass, still half-asleep, held transparent drops within itself, and the bark smelled of rain from many hours before. In such moments the world knew how to look as though it favored nesting. The blackbird descended lower, hopped across the ground in short, alert movements, glanced from side to side, gathered what was fit: thin twigs, dry blades of grass, and the softness of down feathers when he happened to find them along the path. And there were moments when everything that usually resists would soften, briefly. The outline of the nest began to appear. From a loose collection of materials, a shape emerged. From the shape, an interior. From the interior, the promise of warmth that no longer came only from his own body, but might remain within the nest.

Perhaps those moments were the hardest for the blackbird.

Not failure, not collapse, not wind. But that brief moment when a single blade of grass begins to resemble fulfillment. When the world does not yet answer, but no longer stays entirely silent. When one can think, for a moment, that this time it is no longer about effort alone, but about actually dwelling.

And it was precisely then that disruption most often came.

Not always in one form, and never in a way that could be named once and for all. A branch that had seemed strong in the light would soften after a few days of rain. Leaves that looked thick enough from below would prove too sparse once evening fell, letting too much sky remain visible between them, so that the cold entered from above as though the nest had never truly been sheltered at all. Some trunks stood straight and whole, yet rot had already begun its quiet work within them — not enough to bring them down, not enough even to make them seem weak, but enough that any new weight would be carried badly. Some places offered cover and nothing with which to build it: no soft grass nearby, no down caught in bramble, no small materials that could be gathered without long and fruitless searching. At other times the tree itself seemed almost ready, almost willing, almost able to receive what was being made, and yet something in it remained turned elsewhere: an old hollow, a lingering scent, the pressure of other wings in the branches, a memory in the wood that never fully released its claim.

And then there were days when the obstacle belonged neither to branch nor trunk nor weather, but to the very air between them. Noise spreading above the canopies. Trembling air arriving from a distance. Other voices, other songs, other rhythms settling on the leaves like invisible dust. And then even a well-laid form began to tremble, as though it no longer knew whether it wished to remain itself. There are spaces in which nothing falls apart at once, but everything gradually loses the capacity to sound through to the end.

Again and again there was something missing. Again and again the shape could be started, but not finished. Again and again the work returned to the same point: too exposed, too hollow, too poor, too uncertain. The branch held, but not for long. The leaves covered, but not enough. The wood stood, but not cleanly. The place welcomed, but not fully. And after a while it was not any single disappointment that exhausted the blackbird, but the sameness of them, the wearying repetition of almost, almost, almost.

But the blackbird did not mistake longing for entitlement.

He did not believe that every tree owed him a nest. He knew too well that not every branch was made to bear the same weight, and not every place was capable of sheltering the same kind of warmth. He did not ask every hollow to become a home, nor every season to ripen before its time. What wearied him was not refusal itself, but the long nearness of forms that almost seemed able to hold what, in truth, they could not. Not every failure was betrayal. Some places were simply too sparse. Some too burdened. Some too exposed. Some too inwardly divided to keep anything warm for long.

And yet the blackbird himself did not sing in a pure tone.

He carried his own tension. His own weariness. His own fear, which cannot be shaken off by morning light alone. There were moments when he suspected that his very effort was thickening the air. That longing, if it lasts too long without an answer, ceases to be only light and begins to burn too hot. That gathered twigs and feathers become, in themselves, a weight upon the branch, upon the leaves, perhaps even upon the tree itself. Not from ill will. Not from cruelty. From that particular exhaustion born when someone can no longer separate warmth from fever.

So there was no single mistake. No single moment after which one could say: here everything turned. That was what made building heavier. The nests rarely disappeared entirely. More often they could still be seen. They already had a center. They had a shape. They even had, for a moment, the semblance of an interior — but they lacked that layer which cannot be brought in a beak: the world’s consent for what had begun as effort to be allowed to endure.

And then winter came.

Not the kind from children’s pictures, but the real one: with white light that beautifies nothing but sharpens everything, with frost entering beneath the feathers deeper than it should, with a silence so transparent it became painful. Snow settled on the unfinished edges and slowly buried the gaps among the twigs, as though wishing to conceal them — and by doing so revealing them all the more clearly. The blackbird sat for a long time then, and it was not strength he lacked. Strength returns. The body is more faithful than the heart. What he lacked was something harder: a place where he could fold his wings and not lift them again the next morning like a weight he must once more carry alone. To the blackbird, that was the hardest burden to bear. Not the cold itself. Not the work itself. But the eternal half-completion. As though the world kept offering the shape of a home, only to hold it just short of the threshold.

And yet the intention did not die.

That was perhaps the strangest thing in him. Not stubbornness for its own sake. Not the vanity of a builder. Something simpler and deeper at once: the knowledge that the nest has meaning. That not everything living was made only to drift on the wind, only for accidental hollows that give shelter for a single night. That there must exist such an order in which warmth and endurance are not two separate things. One in which different songs do not cancel each other out, but take up a single melody.

Because the blackbird was not only a builder. The blackbird sang, and the blackbird dreamed.

And perhaps that was why he could not content himself with the mere semblance of agreement. He had learned, slowly, that to see a broken branch and name it honestly was not the same as taking upon himself the full weight of the tree. Sometimes it meant only this: that he had been there, that something had been carried, and that he did not wish to pretend otherwise. But whoever carries music within knows, sooner or later, the difference between sounds that simply exist beside one another and a melody that truly gathers itself into one form. It is not that everything must sound the same — quite the opposite. True song is born from difference. But a difference that is to enter a melody cannot be mutual cancellation. It must be able to be heard. Accepted. And perhaps that is why not every closeness becomes a home, not every shared presence passes into shared dwelling, not every warmth can survive longer than a single season.

He did not know whether he would encounter a tree that could hold a nest all the way to the end.

He knew only that he would rather remain faithful to that possibility than learn to call home everything that merely keeps out the cold.

title: Circulation
content:
I am awake in the wrong way.
Awake like a wound that refuses to close.

My jaw is tense. My teeth are grinding.
My hands want to do something small and useless:
clean the windows, straighten a blanket, check the time again - 
as if order could replace closeness.

I know this state.
It always comes when love and hope turn into absence.


There is an outline in the dust where something used to be.

A watch on the bedside table, charging quietly throughout the night.
Two phones face down.
A glass of water half-finished.
Two cables tangled and then separated when the morning would come.

Coffee poured before one of us fully arrived in their own eyes.
Burned edges of toast would be hidden under a layer of jam.
Keys searched for while brushing teeth.
A rushed kiss in the hallway followed by a quick: “Text me when you get there.”

That kind of life.


And still - when I love - I do the same brutal thing.

My mind is precise.
It knows where to cut.

Fingers slip between ribs.
Pressure against cartilage,
The resistance of muscle, the heat of it,
that thick, animal insistence of a heart that still believes.

I reach in.

It does not come out clean.
It drags something with it.
It is heavier than it should be.
It keeps pumping even while it is held in the open air,
as if it cannot accept that it has been removed.

And I place it in someone else’s hands.

Whole.

Because that is what I do:
I don’t offer a spark.
I offer a living organ.

And if it returns - because it always returns -
it looks intact.

Nothing “broken” in the visible sense.
But the ventricles feel hollow.

There was blood here. It's gone now.

It is the strangest pain:
to have your heart handed back to you
as if it is yours again
but it does not contain your life anymore.

So the body improvises.

It pushes new blood, slowly.
It refills what has collapsed inward.
It learns to stand up without dizziness.
It learns to eat without nausea.
To breathe without expecting a door to open.


I am tired of rebuilding circulation alone.

Not because I loved.
But because I keep having to learn the same lesson:

To let go.

I don’t want my life to be a constant act of letting go.

I don’t want to be the person who changes someone’s trajectory
and then remains only as a memory on a shelf.

I don’t want to be a threshold.
A catalyst.
A brief flame that proves something was possible -
and then disappears so the other person can live.

I want to stay.

I want to be the kitchen light left on in the evening.
Green tea cooling on the counter.
A shower together where the mirror fogs up and we both compare the heat of the water.
A forehead pressed into mine gently when it's hard to get out of bed.
Someone mumbling in their sleep.
Someone looking at me first when something good happens.

I want a small world that grows.

Magnets multiplying on the fridge.
More figurines on the shelves.
A second mug that slowly becomes “yours”.
A coat thrown over a chair that slowly stops being “mess” and becomes “home.”

I don't want to keep practicing goodbye as if it were a skill.


My mind can cut.

It dissects because it wants to protect what it offers.
It tries to understand before it commits.
It tries to secure the ground before building.

But sometimes, in trying to perform a clean operation,
I forget that hearts are not meant to be handled under surgical light.

They are meant to remain inside a chest, and beat next to one without incision.

I don't want to keep removing mine.
I don't want to keep watching it relearn how to fill itself.

I want one story
where the heart stays where it belongs
and nothing has to be stitched back together.

But I am afraid my heart will remain connected to the drip,
kept alive just enough not to give up,
not strong enough to run.

As if I were lying in a hospital bed,
looking out of a window,
watching life move forward
while I remain connected to machines
that hum softly
and promise life support
but not life itself.

title: Still a Love
contentHtml:
Is it grief, or something older - this ache of waiting for a closeness that always seemed just beyond the edge of reality?

There are nights when love feels nearest precisely because it has not arrived.
The moon lingers at my window like a thought that never found its ending,
and the stars, in all their quiet distance, resemble the selves I might have become had someone looked long enough to recognize the life beneath my words.

I do not speak of sorrow loudly now. It has softened into something almost livable, woven so carefully through me it sometimes passes for calm. It moves the way evening light moves across an empty room — gentle, unhurried, and harder to bear for being so gentle.

But not every heart is answered according to its depth. Some are touched only briefly, as if what they carry asks for a kind of presence few people know how to give.

And so I have come to know the silence that follows hope: the stillness after a door remains closed, the change in a voice when warmth has quietly left it, the strange work of gathering back all the feeling that had begun to reach outward.

There is something lonely in carrying so much inwardness and finding so little room where it can rest without becoming less. Sometimes I wonder whether I was made not for love itself, but for its outline — for the almost of it, for the brief brightness of being near what might have changed everything, and then the distance that returns leaving the heart more awake and more alone.

Still, I cannot speak of love with bitterness. I think of it too tenderly for that — as one thinks of a season that never fully came, but altered the air enough to make the world feel possible.

And if no one ever knows me in the way I once hoped to be known, let it at least be true that I did not turn away from the softness of that longing. That I kept something unguarded in me, even as life kept asking for distance.

For there is something quietly tragic in being made for nearness and learning instead the language of absence; in having a heart that might have opened under the smallest kindness, and watching it give its color to solitude instead.

Perhaps that is what I am: not unloved exactly, but unanswered — still carrying within me a kind of love that has never found its natural home, so quiet it can almost be mistaken for silence.
